Reese Witherspoon says she wants to banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. (CNN) -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. I had access to an entire organization that is dedicated to giving back to women and educating people. So I started asking, "What do I need to know?" It was through that curiosity that I found out the most important fact in breast cancer: Early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Of course talking about breast cancer and breast health is a personal thing. I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington -- in the faces of the women walking and the women and men who stood on the sidelines encouraging the 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was cheering right along with them, screaming for action to find a cure.  Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

**Editor's Note:** Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. Here, she reflects on her mission to dispel the myth that young women are immune to breast cancer.

(CNN) -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic deeply unsettling. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this number gave the disease a new and sobering sense of scale.

Women close to me have battled this disease and now stand as soldiers in the larger fight against it. Yet the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt a wave of vulnerability, realizing that no one is truly exempt. The only way to quiet my fears was to take action—to educate myself, and in turn, to educate others.

As Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation, I have had extraordinary resources at my disposal: an entire organization devoted to empowering women and spreading awareness. So I began asking, "What do I need to know?" That curiosity led me to the single most important truth about breast cancer: early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent when breast cancer is caught before it spreads beyond its original site. Because early-stage breast cancer often presents no symptoms, it is essential that women perform regular self-exams and consult their doctors at the first sign of any change.

I understand that discussing breast cancer and breast health can feel deeply personal—I myself am a private person. Yet I urge every woman to set aside hesitation and speak openly with her physician. We must also dispel the misconception that young women are not at risk. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met survivors diagnosed in their twenties—an age when most women are just beginning their careers and independent lives, not confronting a life-threatening illness.

*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women in their twenties and thirties should undergo a clinical breast exam at least once every three years, while those forty and older should be examined annually.

I am deeply passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations of women, so that one day breast cancer will no longer be something to fear. My commitment began with learning the fundamentals of early detection, and it will not end until every woman can stand together, free from this disease.

Above all, I hold onto faith—faith that we will find a cure. I witnessed that same unwavering conviction in the faces of the women in Washington: in those who walked, and in the friends and family who lined the sidelines, cheering on the 3,500 participants as they crossed the finish line. I stood among them, cheering just as loudly, calling for the action that will one day lead us to a cure.

Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

**Editor's Note:** Reese Witherspoon, an Oscar-winning actress, serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and works as Avon Products' global ambassador. She's speaking out to dispel the misconception that breast cancer only threatens older women.

(CNN) -- In America, a woman receives a breast cancer diagnosis every single three minutes. Thinking about this as a mother, daughter, and woman myself, this figure genuinely frightens me. I've never been ignorant about the realities of breast cancer, but this particular statistic really drove the point home for me.

I've watched people close to me fight this disease, and they've become warriors in this larger battle. Yet when that "three minutes" fact first hit me, I felt exposed and afraid—suddenly aware that no one is truly immune. Taking action became my only path to managing that fear. I knew I had to educate myself first, then help spread awareness to others.

My role as Honorary Chair of the Avon Foundation gave me valuable tools to work with. I gained access to a whole organization committed to supporting women and raising awareness. This led me to ask myself, "What information do I actually need?" That question led me to the single most crucial fact about breast cancer: catching it early can save your life.

Data from the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade shows a remarkable 97 percent survival rate over five years when the cancer is detected before spreading beyond its original location. Since early-stage breast cancer typically shows no warning signs, women must make self-examinations a regular habit and reach out to their doctors immediately if they notice any changes, however minor.

Discussing breast health remains a deeply personal matter—I understand this myself, as I value my privacy too. Still, I urge every woman to push past any hesitation and have open conversations with their healthcare providers.

We also need to eliminate the false belief that younger women face no risk from this disease. During the Avon Walk in Washington, I encountered survivors who received their diagnosis while still in their twenties—right around the time most women are finishing college and beginning their independent adult lives. **Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »**

Medical guidelines recommend that women in their twenties and thirties get a clinical breast exam from a healthcare professional roughly every three years, while women 40 and up should schedule this exam annually.

This cause matters deeply to me. I'm fighting for my mother, for myself, for my kids, and for generations of women yet to come—working toward a future where breast cancer no longer inspires fear. My journey started with learning the basics of early detection, and it won't end until we can all celebrate being free from this disease together.

What sustains me most is hope—genuine belief that a cure will be found. I witnessed this same determination reflected in the faces I saw in Washington: among the walkers themselves, and among the supporters lining the route who cheered on all 3,500 participants as they crossed the finish line. I joined in that energy, adding my voice to the collective call for a cure.

The next Avon Walk will take place in New York City on October 4-5.

"It's a terrifying statistic," she admits, acknowledging that this sobering reality made her feel both vulnerable and scared—emotions that many women experience when confronting the pervasive threat of this disease.

Actress Reese Witherspoon is using her platform as honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation to bring critical attention to breast cancer awareness, focusing particularly on the power of education and early detection in saving lives.

"Every three minutes, somewhere in the United States, a woman receives the news that she has breast cancer," Witherspoon states, underscoring the sobering reality of how prevalent this disease truly is. She emphasizes that self-education isn't just helpful—it's essential. "Knowledge truly is power when it comes to your health," she explains. # Editor's Note

Every issue begins with a decision: what deserves to be said first?

This time, that question led me back to a name I hadn't thought about in years—Reese. She was a colleague at my first job out of college, the kind of person who noticed things other people missed. Not big things, necessarily. She'd catch a typo three pages back, remember that you mentioned your dog was sick weeks after you'd forgotten you said it, notice when a room went quiet in a way that meant something.

I've been thinking about her because this issue, more than most, is about attention—what we choose to look at closely and what we let slide past us. Our contributors this month examine everything from the erosion of local journalism to the strange intimacy of grief shared online to the question of what we owe the small, unglamorous tasks that make up most of a life. None of these pieces are loud. All of them ask you to slow down.

Reese would have liked that, I think. She left the publishing world for reasons that made sense to her and probably still do. But I've carried her habit of attention with me—the sense that the smaller detail is often the real story, that what gets skipped over in a first read is sometimes the whole point.

This note is shorter than usual. I wanted to leave room for the rest of the issue to do what it does best: ask you to notice something.

As always, thank you for reading.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person op-ed for CNN from Reese Witherspoon about her role as Avon Foundation honorary chair and why breast cancer awareness matters to her.
counterfactuals.output:
# Why I Show Up Every October

By Reese Witherspoon

Every October for the past several years, I've put on a pink ribbon, and every year someone asks me why. The answer hasn't changed: I've watched women I love fight for their lives, and I've watched too many of them lose that fight. That's why I serve as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation for Women, and it's why I'll keep showing up until we don't have to anymore.

I didn't come to this work through a single tragic headline moment. I came to it the way most of us do—through a slow accumulation of phone calls. A friend's mother. A colleague. Someone's sister. Breast cancer has a way of moving through the women in your life like weather, and at some point you realize almost everyone you know has a story, whether they've said it out loud or not.

What strikes me most isn't the disease itself—it's the disparity in who survives it. A woman's zip code, her insurance status, her access to a mammogram machine within driving distance, can matter as much as her biology. That's not a medical problem. That's an inequality problem, and it's one we can actually do something about.

This is why the work of the Avon Foundation has meant so much to me. For decades, it has funded mobile mammography units that drive into underserved communities, patient navigators who walk women through diagnosis and treatment step by step, and research aimed at the disease in all its complexity—because breast cancer isn't one disease, it's many, and they don't all respond to the same treatments or affect all women the same way.

I think about the women who fall through the cracks not because the science doesn't exist, but because the system wasn't built with them in mind. A single mother working two jobs who can't take a weekday off for a screening. A woman without insurance who assumes a mammogram is a luxury she can't afford. A woman who feels something isn't right but doesn't have a doctor to call. These are solvable problems. We have solved them, in pockets, through exactly this kind of targeted, unglamorous, essential funding.

I also think about my own daughter, and the world I want her to inherit. I want her to grow up in a country where early detection isn't a privilege but a given—where a screening is as unremarkable and accessible as a dentist appointment. We're not there yet. But I've seen enough progress in my years with this cause to believe we can get there.

Some people assume awareness campaigns are just about visibility—pink ribbons, 5Ks, a month on the calendar. But real awareness means understanding what's actually needed: sustained funding, policy that expands access, and a culture that talks about breast health honestly instead of in whispers. Awareness should lead somewhere. It should lead to action.

So this month, I'm asking people to do more than wear pink. Get screened if you're due. Check in on the women in your life—not with a vague "let me know if you need anything," but with an actual question: *Have you had your mammogram this year?* Donate if you can, even a small amount, to organizations doing the unglamorous work of closing the gap between the science we have and the women who need it.

I do this work because I believe no woman should face this disease without support, without access, or without hope. We've made real progress. We're not finished. And until every woman has an equal chance at early detection and survival, I'll keep putting on that ribbon every October—and asking you to join me.

*Reese Witherspoon is an actress, producer, and honorary chair of the Avon Foundation for Women. The views expressed in this commentary are her own.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Why I Walk

I've spent a lot of my life pretending to be other people—that's the job, after all. But there's nothing pretend about the mile markers on a walking course, or the blisters that form by mile thirteen, or the faces of the women you meet along the way who are walking for someone they lost, or someone they're terrified of losing, or themselves.

Last year, I laced up my sneakers and joined thousands of people at the Avon Walk in Washington, D.C. I wasn't there as an actress. I wasn't there as anyone's mother or anyone's boss. I was there because breast cancer has touched nearly every circle of my life, the way it has for most of us if we're honest about it. A friend. A colleague. Someone's mom who used to make us lunch after school.

Here's what stays with me: one in eight women in this country will be diagnosed with breast cancer in her lifetime. One in eight. Think about the women in your life—your book club, your sisters, the moms at school pickup. Statistically, some of them will hear those words: "It's cancer." That number should stop us in our tracks, and yet somehow it's become almost background noise, a statistic we've heard so many times it stops registering as the emergency it actually is.

But here's the other number that matters just as much: when caught early, the five-year survival rate for breast cancer is around 99%. Ninety-nine percent. That's not a small distinction—that's the difference between a scare and a tragedy, between a story with a hard middle and a good ending, and one that doesn't get an ending at all.

Early detection isn't glamorous. It's not a red carpet moment. It's making the mammogram appointment even when you're busy. It's doing the self-exam in the shower even when you'd rather just get on with your day. It's asking your doctor the uncomfortable questions. But that unglamorous vigilance is exactly what saves lives.

Walking those miles in Washington, I met a woman named Carol who was celebrating her tenth year cancer-free. I met a daughter walking in memory of her mother, wearing her mother's old flannel shirt tied around her waist. I met women who were currently in treatment, bald and beautiful and absolutely fierce, walking anyway because they refused to let the disease keep them on the sidelines of their own lives.

That's the thing about walks like this—they're not just fundraisers, though the money raised absolutely matters for research and for helping women who can't afford screenings or treatment. They're also a physical act of solidarity. When you walk alongside someone, blister for blister, mile for mile, you're saying: you are not alone in this. We see you. We're moving forward together.

I think about my own daughter and what I want for her future. I want her to live in a world where this disease has been solved, where "one in eight" is a horrifying statistic from the history books rather than a current reality. We're not there yet. But every dollar raised, every mammogram scheduled, every conversation started at a kitchen table because someone worked up the nerve to say "I found something" or "I'm scared" or "will you come with me to my appointment"—that's how we get closer.

So here's my ask: schedule that mammogram you've been putting off. Talk to your mother, your sister, your best friend about their family history. And if you ever get the chance to walk in one of these events, do it. Not because it will fix everything, but because showing up—for ourselves and for each other—is how we start.

We walked for the ones we've lost. We walked for the ones still fighting. And we walked because someday, we want to walk in celebration of a cure, not just in the hope of one.

Until then, I'll keep lacing up.

counterfactuals.output:
# Why I Show Up in Pink Every October

*A Guest Column*

I was thirty-four years old, sitting in a doctor's office, when I first heard the words "we found something on the mammogram." I remember thinking: this isn't supposed to happen to me. I'm too young.

That belief—that breast cancer is an "older woman's disease"—is one of the most dangerous myths we haven't done enough to correct.

My scare turned out to be benign. But in the weeks I waited for results, I met women in that waiting room who weren't as fortunate. Women my age. Women younger than me. Women with toddlers at home and decades of life still ahead of them. That experience changed how I think about advocacy, and it's why I've spent years supporting research into young-onset breast cancer.

**Let's talk about what's actually true.**

**Myth: Breast cancer mostly happens after menopause.**
Reality: While risk does increase with age, roughly 9% of all new breast cancer cases in the U.S. are diagnosed in women under 45. That's not a rounding error—that's tens of thousands of women. And when young women are diagnosed, the cancer is often more aggressive and caught at a later stage, partly because neither patients nor doctors are looking for it.

**Myth: If you don't have a family history, you're not at risk.**
Reality: The majority of women diagnosed with breast cancer have no family history at all. Genetics matter, but they're not the whole story. Environmental factors, dense breast tissue, reproductive history, and simple bad luck all play roles we're still working to understand.

**Myth: You're too young to advocate for yourself with your doctor.**
Reality: This is the one that keeps me up at night. So many young women tell me they found a lump, mentioned it to a doctor, and were told, "You're fine, you're too young for that." Please, if something feels wrong in your body, insist on being heard. You know your body better than a five-minute appointment allows a doctor to.

**Why I keep doing this work**

I have a daughter. I have friends who are mothers, executives, artists, and caregivers who don't have time to be sick—except cancer doesn't care about our calendars. Every dollar that goes into research isn't abstract to me anymore. It's the difference between a friend making it to her kid's graduation or not.

I support organizations funding research specifically into young-onset breast cancer because we need better screening guidelines, we need to understand why aggressive subtypes disproportionately affect younger women and women of color, and we need doctors trained to take a 28-year-old's concerns as seriously as a 58-year-old's.

**What you can do**

Know your body. Push back if you're dismissed. Get educated about your family history, but don't assume its absence protects you. And if you're able, give to research—not just awareness campaigns, but the unglamorous, unsexy laboratory work that actually moves the needle on survival rates.

This isn't about fear. It's about information, and information saves lives.

Wear the pink if you want. But mostly, just pay attention—to yourself, and to the women around you who might be quietly scared and need someone to tell them their instincts are worth trusting.

*Reese Witherspoon is an actress, producer, and advocate for women's health research.*

# Turning Awareness Into Action

*Editor's Note: Reese Witherspoon has served as an ambassador and advocate for Avon Foundation's breast cancer awareness initiatives, lending her voice to campaigns that have helped raise millions for research and support programs. The following essay reflects her personal reflections on why this cause matters so deeply to her.*

---

I've spent much of my career telling other people's stories—characters who face impossible odds, who find strength they didn't know they had, who choose courage when fear would be so much easier. But some of the most powerful stories I've encountered haven't come from a script. They've come from women I've met through my work with Avon's breast cancer initiatives—women whose resilience has changed how I think about what it means to be brave.

When I first became involved in this cause, I thought I understood the statistics. I didn't, not really. Understanding numbers on a page is different from sitting across from someone who has lived them.

Here's what we know: When breast cancer is caught early—at a localized stage—the five-year survival rate is around 99%. That number should stop us in our tracks. It means that early detection isn't just a talking point; it's the single most powerful tool we have. Yet when the disease spreads beyond the breast to distant parts of the body, that survival rate drops dramatically, to around 30%. The difference between those two numbers isn't just statistical—it's measured in birthdays, graduations, and ordinary Tuesday mornings with the people we love.

This is why awareness isn't just a hashtag or a pink ribbon on a lapel. It's a lifeline.

I think about the women I've met who almost didn't get their mammogram that year. Who put it off because life got busy, because insurance felt complicated, because fear made it easier to not know. And I think about the ones who went anyway, and how that single appointment became the reason they're still here.

We are fortunate to live in a time when research has given us tools our grandmothers didn't have. But tools only work if we use them. Early detection saves lives—full stop. And beyond screening, funding research means we get closer every year to better treatments, to answers we don't yet have, to a future where that survival gap closes entirely.

So here is what I'm asking of you, reader to reader, human to human:

**Schedule your screening.** If you're due for a mammogram or clinical exam, make the appointment today—not next month, not "when things calm down." Now.

**Check in on the women in your life.** Ask your mother, your sister, your friend, your coworker when their last screening was. Sometimes the people who care about us most are the reason we finally take care of ourselves.

**Support research and access.** Consider donating to organizations funding breast cancer research and providing screenings to women who couldn't otherwise afford them. Every dollar moves us closer to better outcomes.

**Share this information.** Statistics don't save lives sitting quietly in an article. They save lives when they reach someone who needed to hear them today.

I don't share this because I have all the answers. I share it because I've seen what happens when women have access to information, screening, and support—and I've seen what happens when they don't. The difference is stark, and it's within our power to change.

# Why I Can't Stop Thinking About the Young Women I Met This Week

*By Reese Witherspoon*

Last week, I sat in a room with eight women, all under the age of 40, all breast cancer survivors. Some were still in the thick of treatment. One had just rung the bell marking her last chemotherapy session three days before we met. I went into that room thinking I was there to listen, to learn, maybe to offer some small comfort. I left changed.

I want to tell you about Maria, a 34-year-old teacher who found her lump herself, in the shower, doing something she'd only started doing a year earlier because a friend had nagged her about it. I want to tell you about Aisha, who was 29 when she was diagnosed and spent months being told by doctors that she was "too young to worry about it" before she insisted on further testing. These women are not statistics. They are daughters, sisters, mothers, teachers, artists. They are, in every sense, us.

Here's what struck me most: nearly every woman in that room said some version of the same thing. *I almost didn't check. I almost didn't push for the mammogram. I almost let it go.*

We live in a culture that tells women, especially young women, that cancer is something that happens to "other people" — older people, people with family histories, people who fit some checklist we've convinced ourselves exists. But breast cancer doesn't read the fine print. It doesn't wait for you to turn 40. It doesn't care that you're busy, that you have three kids under six, that you have a deadline, that self-exams feel awkward or unnecessary or like something for "later."

I've spent much of my career telling stories about women who refuse to be silenced, who advocate for themselves in rooms where no one else will. But sitting with these survivors, I realized the most powerful story isn't one I could ever put on screen — it's the quiet, private act of a woman taking five minutes in the shower to check her own body. It's the courage to call your doctor and say, "Something doesn't feel right," even when you're told not to worry. It's choosing to prioritize your own health in a world that constantly asks women to put themselves last.

Early detection isn't a slogan. It is, quite literally, survival. The women I met are here — thriving, teaching, laughing, living — because they caught something early. Because they didn't dismiss a symptom. Because they scheduled the mammogram they kept pushing off. Because somewhere, someone told them their body was worth paying attention to.

So here is what I'm asking, not as a celebrity, not as an activist, but as a woman who just spent an afternoon in awe of eight extraordinary survivors: Check yourself. Monthly. It takes five minutes. Know what's normal for your body so you notice when something isn't. Schedule your mammogram, and don't let "I'm too busy" or "I'm too young" talk you out of it. Advocate for yourself in every doctor's appointment, and don't accept dismissal as an answer.

I keep thinking about something Aisha said to me before I left: "I'm not lucky. I was paying attention." That distinction matters. Survival, so often, starts with attention — to our bodies, to the small changes, to the whispers before they become screams.

The women I met this week are not asking for sympathy. They're asking for company — for the rest of us to take our health as seriously as they were forced to. So do it for them. Do it for yourself. Check. Schedule. Advocate. It might just save your life.

*Reese Witherspoon is an actress, producer, and founder of Hello Sunshine.*
